summary: How international and UK aviation law fit together. ICAO and the Chicago Convention set the Articles on sovereignty, registration, documents and licences, with 19 Annexes behind them. EASA and the UK CAA regulate at regional and national level. The UK Aeronautical Information Service covers the AIP and its 28-day AIRAC cycle, colour-coded AICs, NOTAMs and Air Supplements, plus the CAP guides and the layout of the Air Navigation Order 2016.
sections: International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)
Civil aviation resumed in 1919; overflying other nations' territory and landing safely at prepared airfields had to be solved
Paris Convention 1919: first major international aviation meeting (mostly European nations); general principles of air law and procedures agreed
Chicago Convention 1944: moral obligation on contracting states to provide safe and efficient ground and flight organisations
ICAO formed 1947, based in Montreal, Canada, to promote standards and recommended practices
The UK, like most nations, is an active ICAO member
Differences between ICAO nations
Cruising levels: feet in western nations, metres in some eastern European nations
Pressure: the UK uses hectopascals (hPa), an ICAO recommendation; the US uses inches of mercury
Airspace classes are widely adopted with small differences: the UK has no Class B, while the USA allocates it to Terminal Control Areas
Chicago Convention principles
The principles are known as Articles
Shall means must (required)
Should means not required, but recommended for good airmanship and flight safety
Articles 1 to 13: sovereignty and regulations
1 Sovereignty: each state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over its airspace
2 Territory: land and waters under a state's sovereignty
4 Misuse: civil aviation not to be used contrary to the convention's aims (illegal uses or war)

5 Non-scheduled flight: aircraft of other states may fly into or through, and land, without prior permission; a state may require overflying aircraft to land, or to follow prescribed routes or get permission where terrain is remote
10 Customs airports: a state may require landing at a customs airport on entry, and departure from one
11 Applicability: any aircraft, whatever its nationality, obeys the regulations of the state it is in

12 Rules of the air: apply to aircraft in a state's territory and aircraft carrying its nationality mark anywhere; over the high seas the convention's rules apply; states endeavour to prosecute violators
13 Entry and clearance: immigration, passport, customs and quarantine rules apply to passengers, crew and cargo
Articles 16 to 26: registration and formalities
16 Search: a state may search aircraft of other states on landing or before departure and inspect documents
17 Nationality: that of the state of registration
18 Dual registration: not allowed, but registration can be changed from one state to another
19 National laws: registration follows that state's laws
20 Marks: aircraft operating internationally display nationality and registration marks
22 Facilitation: prevent unnecessary delays (customs, immigration, quarantine)
23 Procedures: customs and immigration follow international practice

24 Customs duty: temporary admission duty-free; fuel, oil, spares and regular equipment retained on board on departure are exempt, but not items unloaded; spares imported for an aircraft on international operations are duty-free
25 Distress: states assist aircraft in distress and allow the owner and state of registry to assist
26 Accident investigation: the state where an accident occurs (deaths, serious injury or serious defect) investigates per ICAO procedures; the state of registry may observe
Articles 28 to 40: facilities, documents and licences
28 Facilities: radio, met and navigation services to ICAO standards; standard systems for communications, marking, signals and lighting; cooperation on charts

29 Documents: certificate of registration, certificate of airworthiness, licence for each crew member, journey logbook, radio licences, passenger list (names, embarkation, destination) if carrying passengers, cargo manifest and declarations if carrying cargo
30 Radio: only if licensed by the state of registry, used per the regulations of the state flown over, and only by licensed crew
31 Certificate of airworthiness: valid, issued by the state of registry
32 Licences: issued by the state of registry; a state may refuse to recognise its own nationals' licences granted by another state for flights over its territory
33 Recognition: certificates and licences recognised if issued to ICAO standards
34 Journey logbooks: kept on international operations
35 Cargo: weapons or munitions of war only with the state's permission; other items may be prohibited for public order or safety
36 Photography: may be prohibited or regulated
37 Standards: states aim for uniformity; ICAO adopts and amends standards and recommended practices (SARPs)
39 and 40 Endorsements: failures to meet a standard are shown on the certificate or licence; use internationally only if permitted; use in another state is at that state's discretion
Articles 43 to 47, Annexes
43: ICAO is formed by the convention, made up of an assembly, a council and other bodies

44 Objectives: safe and orderly growth; peaceful aircraft design and operation; development of airways, airports and navigation facilities; safe, regular, efficient and economical transport; fair competition without discrimination
47: states grant ICAO the legal capacity it needs
19 Annexes supplement the articles and define standards and recommended practices (SARPs)
UK differences from the ICAO system are shown in AIP GEN 1-7
EASA
EASA regulates licensing for pilots and aircraft across the EU, with full responsibility for flight operations and crew licensing (including training)
Having left the EU, the UK is again responsible for its own regulation
Key regulations for private pilots: the Basic Regulation and the Aircrew Regulation, both amended regularly
The Basic Regulation has annexes on airworthiness, licensing, medical and air traffic management
Subdivisions are Parts (e.g. Part ORA covers organisations such as training schools), implemented through AMC (Acceptable Means of Compliance) and GM (Guidance Material)
Aviation law in the UK
Enacted by Parliament; main sources for a private pilot: the Air Navigation Order, Part-NCO, Part-FCL and the Air Navigation (General) Regulations
The CAA is responsible for civil aviation in the UK, including the Aeronautical Information Service (AIS)
Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP)
GEN: national regulations and requirements, services, charges
ENR: en route rules and procedures, ATS information, navigation warnings
AD: information on licensed UK aerodromes
Updated on a fixed 28-day AIRAC cycle (Aeronautical Information Regulation And Control), with information of lasting character
Aeronautical Information Circulars (AICs)
Published monthly: administrative matters, advance warning of operational changes, operational and safety advice
Colours: Air Safety pink; Administrative white; Operational and Air Traffic Services yellow; UK Restrictions Chart mauve; Maps/Charts green

The exam may refer to a specific AIC; read the relevant ones, especially pink: Take-off, Climb and Landing Performance (AIC 127/2006, Pink 110), Wake Turbulence (AIC P083/2020), Helicopter Flight in Degraded Visual Conditions (AIC P137/2019)
NOTAMs and Air Supplements
NOTAMs are obtained daily before flight: restrictions (temporary controlled airspace, Red Arrows displays), runway closures, temporary obstacles, other vital information
Categories: NOTAMN new, NOTAMR replaces a previous one, NOTAMC cancels a previous one
Air Supplements carry temporary information with too much text or graphics for a NOTAM, e.g. major air shows or aerodrome work
AIP Supplements are issued every 28 days and stay current until no longer valid or notified as such
AIS delivery and publications
NATS provides the AIS on behalf of the CAA (NATS AIS Internet Briefing System)
AIS is giving way to the digital Aeronautical Information Management (AIM) system; ICAO Annex 15 covers aeronautical information services
CAP 1535 Skyway Code; CAP 637 Visual aids handbook; CAP 413 Radiotelephony procedures; CAP 804 licence requirements (reference only)
CAA General Aviation Safety Leaflets are available at training organisations and aeroclubs
The Air Navigation Order 2016
A statutory instrument enacted by Parliament as the basis of UK civil aviation, arranged in Parts (e.g. Part 4 Airworthiness of Aircraft) with consecutively numbered Articles
Further detail is in Schedules (e.g. Schedule 1 Interpretation)
Flight planners refer to it for equipment, licensing, documents, registration and operations, alongside Part-NCO
Schedule 13 sets liability and maximum penalties for contraventions
Schedule 1 gives the legal definitions and acts as a glossary

sum.International Civil Aviation Organisatio: Post-WW1 flying led to the Paris Convention (1919), the Chicago Convention (1944) and ICAO (1947, Montreal) to set common standards.
sum.Differences between ICAO nations: Nations differ on cruising level units, pressure units and airspace classes; the UK uses feet, hPa and has no Class B.
sum.Chicago Convention principles: Its principles are called Articles; "shall" is mandatory and "should" is only recommended.
sum.Articles 1 to 13: sovereignty and regula: States control their own airspace and regulations; any aircraft must obey the rules of the state it is in, and customs and entry rules apply.
sum.Articles 16 to 26: registration and form: An aircraft has one nationality (its state of registry), shows its marks, benefits from smooth customs, and is investigated by the state where an accident occurs.
sum.Articles 28 to 40: facilities, documents: Covers the facilities states provide and the documents, licences and certificates needed for international flights, which are recognised if they meet ICAO standards.
sum.Articles 43 to 47, Annexes: Sets up ICAO, its objectives and legal capacity; 19 Annexes hold the detailed standards, with UK differences in AIP GEN 1-7.
sum.EASA: EASA regulated licensing and operations across the EU; the UK now regulates itself, but the Parts, AMCs and GM structure remains familiar.
sum.Aviation law in the UK: UK law comes from Parliament via the ANO, Part-NCO, Part-FCL and the General Regulations, with the CAA responsible for information through the AIS.
sum.Aeronautical Information Publication (AI: The AIP has three parts (GEN, ENR, AD) and is revised every 28 days on the AIRAC cycle.
sum.Aeronautical Information Circulars (AICs: Monthly circulars on administration, operations and safety, colour-coded by subject; pink safety AICs matter most for the exam.
sum.NOTAMs and Air Supplements: NOTAMs give daily short-notice information (new, replacing or cancelling); Air Supplements carry longer temporary information.
sum.AIS delivery and publications: NATS delivers the AIS for the CAA, AIM is replacing it, and the CAPs and safety leaflets explain the rules in simpler form.
sum.The Air Navigation Order 2016: The ANO is the UK's main aviation statute: Parts and Articles for the rules, Schedules for detail, penalties in Schedule 13 and definitions in Schedule 1.

cards.q: What was the Paris Convention of 1919?
cards.a: The first major international aviation meeting, mostly European nations. It agreed general principles of air law and procedures.

cards.q: What did the Chicago Convention (1944) establish?
cards.a: A moral obligation on contracting states to provide safe and efficient ground and flight organisations.

cards.q: When was ICAO formed, and where is it based?
cards.a: 1947, Montreal, Canada.

cards.q: What is ICAO's purpose?
cards.a: To promote aviation standards and recommended practices internationally.

cards.q: Cruising level units: west vs some eastern Europe?
cards.a: Feet in the west; metres in some eastern European nations.

cards.q: Pressure units: UK vs US?
cards.a: UK: hectopascals (hPa). US: inches of mercury.

cards.q: How does UK airspace differ on Class B?
cards.a: The UK has no Class B. In the USA it is allocated to Terminal Control Areas.

cards.q: What are ICAO principles from the Chicago Convention called?
cards.a: Articles.

cards.q: ICAO wording: shall vs should?
cards.a: Shall means must (required). Should means recommended for good airmanship and safety, not required.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article gives each state complete and exclusive sovereignty over its airspace?
cards.a: Article 1 (sovereignty).
cards.m: The number one rule: my sky.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article lets non-scheduled flights fly into or across a state without prior permission?
cards.a: Article 5 (non-scheduled flights). The state may still require the aircraft to land.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article says an aircraft must obey the laws and regulations of the state it is in, whatever its nationality?
cards.a: Article 11 (obey local regulations).

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article covers rules of the air, including which rules apply over the high seas?
cards.a: Article 12 (rules of the air). States keep their rules as close as possible to ICAO's; over the high seas ICAO's rules apply.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which articles say an aircraft takes the nationality of its state of registration, and cannot be registered in two states at once?
cards.a: Articles 17 (nationality) and 18 (no dual registration). Registration can still be changed from one state to another.
cards.m: 17 and 18 are a pair: registered means nationality, and only one state at a time.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article requires aircraft on international flights to display nationality and registration marks?
cards.a: Article 20 (display of marks).

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article makes fuel, oil, spares and regular equipment on board exempt from customs duty on arrival?
cards.a: Article 24 (customs duty). Items unloaded are not exempt.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article says who investigates an accident in another state?
cards.a: Article 26 (accident investigation). The state where it happens investigates; the state of registry may send observers.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article lists the documents carried on international flights, and what are they?
cards.a: Article 29. Certificate of registration, certificate of airworthiness, crew licences, journey log book, radio station licence, passenger list and cargo manifest (if carrying them). Not the pilot's personal logbook.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article requires a certificate of airworthiness for international flights?
cards.a: Article 31. Issued or validated by the state of registry.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which articles cover crew licences and their recognition by other states?
cards.a: Articles 32 (licences issued or validated by the state of registry) and 33 (other states recognise them if they meet ICAO standards).
cards.m: 32: who is flying it? 33: everyone accepts them.

cards.q: Chicago Convention: which article sets out ICAO's objectives?
cards.a: Article 44. Develop international air navigation and foster safe, orderly growth of international air transport: peaceful use, fair competition, no discrimination.

cards.q: How many ICAO Annexes, and where are UK differences shown?
cards.a: 19 Annexes. UK differences are in AIP GEN 1-7.

cards.q: Who regulates UK aviation after leaving the EU, and what is the CAA's information role?
cards.a: The UK regulates itself. The CAA provides the Aeronautical Information Service (AIS), delivered by NATS.

cards.q: What are AMC and GM?
cards.a: Acceptable Means of Compliance and Guidance Material, used to implement the rules in Parts.

cards.q: What is Part ORA?
cards.a: The Part dealing with regulation of organisations, such as training schools.

cards.q: Main UK sources of regulation for a private pilot?
cards.a: The Air Navigation Order, Part-NCO, Part-FCL and the Air Navigation (General) Regulations.

cards.q: What do the AIP parts GEN, ENR and AD cover?
cards.a: GEN: national regulations and services. ENR: en route information. AD: licensed aerodromes.

cards.q: How often is the AIP updated?
cards.a: Every 28 days on the AIRAC cycle.

cards.q: How often are AICs published, and what is the colour code?
cards.a: Monthly. Pink air safety, white administrative, yellow operational/ATS, mauve UK restrictions chart, green maps/charts.

cards.q: NOTAM categories?
cards.a: NOTAMN new, NOTAMR replacing, NOTAMC cancelling.

cards.q: What are Air Supplements?
cards.a: Temporary information with too much text or graphics for a NOTAM, e.g. air shows or aerodrome work. Issued every 28 days.

cards.q: What is replacing the AIS concept?
cards.a: The digital Aeronautical Information Management (AIM) system. ICAO Annex 15 covers aeronautical information services.
Skyway Code; Visual aids handbook; Radiotelephony procedures; licence requirements (reference only).

cards.q: How is the ANO 2016 organised?
cards.a: Parts containing consecutively numbered Articles, with detail in Schedules.

cards.q: ANO Schedule 13 and Schedule 1?
cards.a: Schedule 13: liability and maximum penalties. Schedule 1: legal definitions (glossary).

quiz.q: Which convention was the first major international aviation meeting?
quiz.why: The Paris Convention of 1919, mostly European nations.

quiz.q: When was ICAO formed?
quiz.why: The Chicago Convention was 1944, ICAO itself was formed in 1947.

quiz.q: Which unit of pressure does the UK use?
quiz.why: The UK uses hPa; the US uses inches of mercury.

quiz.q: Which airspace class does the UK not have?
quiz.why: The UK has no Class B; in the USA it covers Terminal Control Areas.

quiz.q: What does 'shall' mean in ICAO documents?
quiz.why: Shall means must. Should is a recommendation.

quiz.q: Which Article gives states exclusive sovereignty over their airspace?
quiz.why: Article 1 is sovereignty.

quiz.q: Which Article makes any aircraft obey the regulations of the state it is in?
quiz.why: Article 11, regardless of nationality.

quiz.q: What nationality does an aircraft have?
quiz.why: Article 17: the state of registration.

quiz.q: Can an aircraft be registered in two states at once?
o: No, but registration can be changed
quiz.why: Article 18 forbids dual registration.

quiz.q: Which Article lists documents carried on international flights?
quiz.why: Article 29.

quiz.q: Which state investigates an accident with deaths in another state?
quiz.why: Article 26: the state where it occurs investigates; the state of registry may observe.

quiz.q: How many ICAO Annexes are there?
quiz.why: There are 19 Annexes.

quiz.q: Where are UK differences from ICAO shown?
quiz.why: AIP GEN 1-7.

quiz.q: How often is the AIP updated?
quiz.why: On the 28-day AIRAC cycle.

quiz.q: What colour are Air Safety AICs?
quiz.why: Pink; white is administrative, yellow operational/ATS, mauve restrictions chart, green maps/charts.

quiz.q: Which AIP part covers licensed aerodromes?
quiz.why: AD covers aerodromes.

quiz.q: What does NOTAMC do?
quiz.why: NOTAMN is new, NOTAMR replaces, NOTAMC cancels.

quiz.q: Which CAP is the radiotelephony procedures guide?
quiz.why: CAP 413. CAP 1535 is the Skyway Code.

quiz.q: Which ANO schedule covers penalties?
quiz.why: Schedule 13; Schedule 1 is interpretation.

quiz.q: Which body is responsible for civil aviation in the UK?
quiz.why: The CAA; NATS provides AIS on its behalf.

quiz.q: How often are AICs published?
quiz.why: AICs are monthly.

quiz.q: What carries temporary information too long for a NOTAM?
quiz.why: Air Supplements, e.g. for major air shows.
